articles.title: Freightos cuts Q3 losses as revenue reaches $7.8 million
articles.summary: Freightos reported revenue of US$7.8 million for the third quarter of 2026, up 2% year-on-year, while significantly reducing its losses through cost-saving measures. The digital freight booking platform recorded an IFRS net loss of US$2.3 million, compared with US$5 million in the same period last year. Its adjusted...
articles.body: Freightos reported revenue of US$7.8 million for the third quarter of 2026, up 2% year-on-year, while significantly reducing its losses through cost-saving measures. The digital freight booking platform recorded an IFRS net loss of US$2.3 million, compared with US$5 million in the same period last year. Its adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed by 52% to US$1.3 million, from US$2.6 million a year earlier. The improvement follows a cost optimisation programme announced in March. The programme has now achieved US$4.8 million in annualised savings, exceeding the company’s original target of US$4.5 million. Freight booking activity continues to grow Freightos processed 494,000 transactions during the quarter, an increase of 15% compared with the previous year. Gross Booking Value (GBV) reached a record US$437 million, up 30%. The company attributed part of the increase to higher freight rates amid tighter capacity and rising fuel costs. The platform also recorded approximately 21,900 unique buyer users, representing year-on-year growth of 6%. Meanwhile, the number of active carriers reached 79, compared with 77 in the third quarter of 2025. Platform revenue increased by 16% to US$3 million. However, revenue from the company’s Solutions business declined by 6% to US$4.8 million. “Our third quarter results demonstrate continued execution against the priorities we established earlier this year: strengthening operational discipline, improving our cost structure, and modernizing our offering to support long-term growth,” said Pablo Pinillos, CEO of Freightos. “We have delivered the cost savings we targeted, significantly narrowing our Adjusted EBITDA loss as we approach breakeven,” Pinillos added. Earlier in November, Freightos also introduced a new version of its Freightos for Forwarders platform, combining pricing, quoting, booking and market intelligence with AI-enabled workflows. Freightos announces share repurchase programme Alongside its financial results, Freightos announced that its board had authorised a share repurchase programme worth up to US$1.7 million. The company may repurchase shares through open-market transactions or other permitted arrangements. The timing and amount of purchases will depend on market conditions and capital requirements. The announcement follows a recent notification from Nasdaq that Freightos no longer meets the exchange’s minimum bid price requirement. The notification does not immediately affect the company’s listing or trading activities. Looking ahead, Freightos expects fourth-quarter revenue of between US$7.6 million and US$7.8 million. For the full year, revenue is forecast to reach US$30.2 million to US$30.4 million, while the adjusted EBITDA loss is expected to range between US$6.9 million and US$7.2 million. The company also expects between 500,000 and 507,000 platform transactions during the final quarter of 2026. Freightos ended September with US$22.3 million in cash, cash equivalents and short-term bank deposits as it continues working towards improved profitability.

articles.title: Samsung Heavy Industries and DNV partner on nuclear-powered LNG carrier
articles.summary: Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI), Tesser Atomics, NTNU and DNV have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to develop a nuclear-powered LNG carrier concept. The project will explore the design of a demonstration vessel intended to operate between LNG terminals in the United States and Europe. The agreement was...
articles.body: Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI), Tesser Atomics, NTNU and DNV have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to develop a nuclear-powered LNG carrier concept. The project will explore the design of a demonstration vessel intended to operate between LNG terminals in the United States and Europe. The agreement was signed at DNV’s headquarters in Høvik, Norway. It brings together expertise in shipbuilding, nuclear technology, maritime safety and academic research. The partners will initially develop a roadmap covering the vessel’s design, safety assessments and regulatory approval requirements. Their long-term objective is to establish a practical pathway towards the construction and operation of a nuclear-powered commercial cargo vessel. Project to explore marine nuclear reactor technology The proposed LNG carrier will be designed around a fluoride-salt-cooled nuclear reactor developed by Tesser Atomics. Samsung Heavy Industries will lead the vessel’s design and the integration of the nuclear power system. It will also examine construction methods and shipbuilding feasibility. Tesser Atomics will focus on reactor development, nuclear safety and licensing requirements. DNV will provide expertise in maritime safety, risk assessment and classification. Meanwhile, NTNU will coordinate research activities, funding proposals and technical studies. The project will also support SFI SAINT, Norway’s research centre focused on nuclear-powered vessels. “Nuclear-powered vessels are one of the promising eco-friendly alternatives for transportation amid the global trend toward decarbonization,” said Kyunghee Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of the Future Business Division, Samsung Heavy Industries. Kim added that the partnership would build on the shipbuilder’s experience with marine small modular reactors and support progress towards commercial applications. Technology could extend to containerships Although the initial project focuses on an LNG carrier, the partners believe the technology could eventually be applied to containerships and other commercial vessels. The research will examine the technical and regulatory challenges associated with introducing nuclear propulsion into merchant shipping. “One of the interesting things about nuclear power for shipping is that we have a long track record of use in the naval segment, but that this has not translated into the commercial sector,” said Ivar Håberg, Director of Approval Ship Classification, DNV. Håberg described the project as an important step towards developing a modern, full-scale nuclear-powered cargo vessel. The partners have not announced a construction contract, investment value or delivery schedule. The initiative remains at the concept development stage, with feasibility studies and safety assessments expected to inform the next steps.

November 23, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Grispb Cameron Brown has been designated as the FMC’s Managing Director and appointed to be a member of the Senior Executive Service. As Managing Director, Mr. Brown implements the administrative directives of the Chairman and coordinates the FMC’s program offices and bureaus. Before joining the Federal Maritime Commission as Managing Director, Mr. Brown worked for several federal agencies over the last two decades in leadership, policymaking, and attorney positions. Most recently, Mr. Brown served as the Deputy Executive Director for Mission at the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board (PCLOB), where he led the agency’s staff in conducting oversight of federal counterterrorism programs. Prior to his work at PCLOB, he served in multiple roles at the Department of Homeland Security. He was the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) Acting Principal Deputy Chief Counsel on multiple occasions, with responsibility for all the agency’s attorneys and the full range of legal services that go into running CISA. Earlier, he worked in attorney and policymaker positions focused on implementing and enforcing the Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards regulatory program. He also served as the Deputy Assistant Administrator for Headquarters Operations at the Department of the Treasury’s Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, where he led a large organization conducting rulemakings, reviewing regulatory filings, conducting international engagement, and operating scientific laboratories. Mr. Brown holds a B.S. from Cornell University and a J.D. from the University of Virginia School of Law. He is originally from northern New York, growing up near the St. Lawrence Seaway. Mr. Brown assumed the Managing Director position in October, 2026.

articles.title: World Shipping Council calls for global agreement on shipping emissions as industry investment surpasses $200 billion USD
articles.summary: The World Shipping Council (WSC) is calling on governments to agree on binding global greenhouse gas regulations for international shipping without further delay, warning that continued uncertainty risks slowing investment in cleaner fuels and infrastructure. As the next round of negotiations get underway at the...
articles.body: World Shipping Council calls for global agreement on shipping emissions as industry investment surpasses $200 billion USD in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 24/11/2026 The World Shipping Council (WSC) is calling on governments to agree on binding global greenhouse gas regulations for international shipping without further delay, warning that continued uncertainty risks slowing investment in cleaner fuels and infrastructure. As the next round of negotiations get underway at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), WSC has identified three elements it considers essential to an effective agreement that delivers on the commitments governments made under the 2023 GHG Strategy: • A credible pathway to net zero, with clear and predictable emissions reduction requirements aligned with the IMO’s 2023 GHG Strategy’s ambition. • Strong and consistent enforcement, ensuring the same rules apply to every ship from the first year. • Incentives for cleaner fuels, helping close the price gap between conventional fuels and zero and near-zero greenhouse gas fuels. The call builds on a joint statement issued by nine major international shipping associations, including WSC, ahead of the IMO negotiations. Representing the global commercial shipping fleet, the associations urged governments to agree on effective and enforceable global regulations that provide investment certainty, incentivise cleaner fuels and maintain a level playing field across international shipping. For the liner industry specifically, investment is already well underway. Container shipping and vehicle carriers have committed more than USD $200 billion to over 1,350 dual-fuel ships, including over 500 already operating. These investments show the industry’s readiness to transition, but unlocking their full emissions reduction potential depends on the availability and commercial competitiveness of cleaner fuels. “Shipping companies are investing billions in ships capable of running on cleaner fuels. We need global rules that give fuel producers and shipowners the confidence to invest in the next stage of the transition,” said Joe Kramek, President & CEO of WSC. “Clear targets, effective enforcement and meaningful incentives for cleaner fuels must work together. An agreement that delivers all three can accelerate progress towards net zero and help turn the investment already underway into real emissions reductions.” WSC cautions that further delays or a framework focused primarily on experience building or fuel market readiness would prolong uncertainty rather than support the transition. Without a meaningful global framework, shipping risks facing a growing patchwork of national and regional emissions regulations, adding complexity and costs to international trade. Since the IMO’s decision to delay adoption of the global agreement, several national shipping carbon charging schemes have been introduced or advanced, underscoring the urgency of reaching a common global regulation. “We believe IMO Member States can work together to reach an agreement that delivers on the commitments made in 2023. As an industry, we will be responsible for implementing the rules agreed at the IMO. That’s why we are calling for clear reduction targets, consistent enforcement and meaningful incentives for cleaner fuels. These are the foundations of an effective global framework that can deliver real emissions reductions,” said Joe Kramek. The World Shipping Council represents the liner shipping industry, which transports about 60 percent of the value of global seaborne trade. • Incentives for cleaner fuels, helping close the price gap between conventional fuels and zero and near-zero greenhouse gas fuels.

articles.title: LPG Carriers: VLGC Earnings Surge to Record High
articles.summary: Disrupted Middle Eastern supplies, robust Asian demand and longer-haul US exports are driving LPG freight rates to unprecedented levels, boosting VLGC earnings. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “this week’s spotlight is on the LPG carriers, as VLGC earnings are at exceptional levels. The...
articles.body: LPG Carriers: VLGC Earnings Surge to Record High in Hellenic Shipping News 24/11/2026 D isrupted Middle Eastern supplies, robust Asian demand and longer-haul US exports are driving LPG freight rates to unprecedented levels, boosting VLGC earnings. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “this week’s spotlight is on the LPG carriers, as VLGC earnings are at exceptional levels. The trade is also now attracting capacity from the broader gas segment: the ACS SP Nereus, a 100k cbm VLEC, has loaded the first LPG cargo for its ship type at Houston. Rates on the US routes surpassed the record-high levels of September 2023 and the summer of 2026 this week, as fixture activity in the West held steady. Houston to Chiba is currently traded at about a TCE return of $184,600/day and Houston to Flushing at approximately $233,600/day TCE”. Source: Intermodal shipbroker According to Intermodal’s Research Analyst, Mr. Vasilis Fousekis, “behind these earnings lies the continued loss of Middle East supply. Hormuz has remained effectively under geopolitical uncertainty in November, with talks on a reopening yet to produce an agreement. Volumes remain below 50% of pre-war levels and Red Sea loadings remain exposed to further attacks. Long haul US cargoes, therefore, have become the main replacement for lost Middle East supply for Asian buyers, keeping the Baltic LPG index to 21k territory, above the Q3 average”. “Vessel availability, rather than export capacity, had so far set the pace of US flows, which are crucial for the LPG trade. A constraint has since emerged on the supply side. Phillips 66, a US based company which operates the Freeport LPG export terminal in Texas, declared force majeure on butane loadings after a power outage and compressor failure incident in early November, lifting US butane prices and raising concern over prompt availability, although overall US LPG loadings have so far shown no clear slowdown. A prolonged outage would mainly tighten butane supply to Asian buyers, rather than reduce the number of cargoes available to fix. In Asia, demand remains firm and at the same time price sensitive. Chinese imports rose by about 1m tonnes q-o-q in Q3, supported by positive margins at propane-to-propylene plants. India consumed 2.6m tonnes in October, approaching the monthly volumes seen before the Middle East conflict, while holiday-season inventory building may extend import strength into November and December. However, if spot prices of propane and butane remain elevated, further buying by Indian importers is likely to slow, especially without any state support”, Mr. Fousekis said. Source: Intermodal shipbroker Meanwhile, “on the supply side, the outlook is less comfortable, with 8 VLGCs delivered within Q3 and 3 more expected within Q4. About 170 VLGC and VLAC newbuildings, totalling 15.5m cbm, are due through 2030, equivalent to roughly 40% of the existing fleet. Contracting has continued at a strong pace, with 8.5m cbm of LPG carriers ordered in the first nine months and a further 14 large gas carriers signed in October. With the fleet averaging about 11.7 years, demolition is unlikely to offset much of this growth”, he added. “Looking ahead, long-haul US exports and Asian restocking should keep earnings well supported in the near term, despite periodic corrections. Seaborne volumes are expected to fall by around 12% this year, yet longer voyages should still lift tonne-miles by about 2.5%. High rates are also drawing marginal tonnage into the market, as the Nereus lifting shows, although such crossovers are likely to stay occasional, mainly when ethane employment is weak. The orderbook is a more significant source of new capacity. A potential settlement of the Hormuz crisis should support the rebound projected for 2027, but a possible recovery in Middle East exports would also shorten average voyages, just as deliveries accelerate in 2027 and 2028. The key question is whether US export growth can absorb that tonnage once trade routes normalize, with the timing of a settlement between Iran and the U.S. remaining the decisive factor”, Intermodal’s analyst concluded. articles.title: Advancing LNG carrier design at scale
articles.summary: Shandong Marine Energy is expanding its LNG carrier portfolio with advanced vessel technologies designed to improve efficiency and safety, working closely with shipyards, technology suppliers, and classification partner DNV. Shandong Marine Energy entered LNG transportation after more than a decade of building...
articles.body: Advancing LNG carrier design at scale in International Shipping News 24/11/2026 S handong Marine Energy is expanding its LNG carrier portfolio with advanced vessel technologies designed to improve efficiency and safety, working closely with shipyards, technology suppliers, and classification partner DNV. Shandong Marine Energy entered LNG transportation after more than a decade of building experience across the liquefied gas shipping sector. “From the very beginning, we had a clear aspiration to enter LNG transportation, the most technically complex and operationally demanding segment of gas shipping,” says Dehua Sun, General Manager of Shandong Marine Energy (SDME). “Building this capability is important not only for our development as a company, but also for strengthening LNG supply chain resilience and supporting long-term energy supply requirements.” Its move into LNG gathered momentum in 2022, when the company acquired the 137,000-cubic-metre Shandong Junbo. Since then, SDME has pursued larger LNG carrier projects linked to major energy companies, including 175,000 cbm vessels for Sinopec and long-term charter agreements with QatarEnergy covering six 174,000 cbm carriers and three 271,000 cbm QC-Max vessels. A further project with Minsheng Financial Leasing, Shell, and Jiangnan Shipyard covers four 175,000 cbm LNG carriers that will provide long-term transportation services for Shell. New LNG carrier designs focus on efficiency SDME’s recently ordered or under-construction LNG carriers range from 174,000 to 271,000 cubic metres, with different designs selected to suit individual operating profiles. Across the fleet, the focus is on improving cargo containment, propulsion efficiency, and hydrodynamic performance. The 175,000 cbm vessels under construction at Jiangnan Shipyard feature GTT Mark III Flex membrane containment technology, with a guaranteed boil-off rate of 0.085 per cent V/day. The much larger QC-Max vessels use the GTT NO96 Super+ containment system and a five-tank configuration, with a design expected to achieve a Carbon Intensity Indicator 23 per cent lower than a standard 174,000 cbm design. “When developing these vessels, we are looking at the vessel as a whole, from cargo containment and propulsion to energy-saving technologies,” explains Sun. “The objective is to improve efficiency and environmental performance while ensuring each vessel suits its intended trade.” Dual-fuel engines and air lubrication reduce emissions Propulsion technology is a key part of this approach. The new vessels use WinGD’s X-DF2.0 low-speed dual-fuel platform, in X72DF-2.1 and X72DF-2.2 variants, with Intelligent Control by Exhaust Recycling (iCER) and variable compression ratio technologies. According to SDME, these technologies can reduce methane slip by more than 50 per cent compared with first-generation X-DF engines, with the lowest levels reaching approximately 0.5–0.7 per cent. LNG dual-fuel auxiliary engines and permanent magnet shaft generators offer additional energy-efficiency gains. These propulsion technologies are complemented by hydrodynamic measures. Both the QC-Max ships and the 175,000 cbm vessels use twin-skeg hull forms, high-efficiency propellers, and a twisted rudder with a rudder bulb. Silverstream air lubrication systems are expected to deliver deliver fuel and emissions savings. Against a standard 174,000 cbm design, the QC-Max ships are designed for 9.9 per cent lower energy consumption per tonne-nautical mile, according to the shipyard’s figures. Safety starts at the LNG carrier design stage For SDME, these efficiency gains cannot come at the expense of safety. Safety is considered throughout the vessel’s life cycle, from evaluating vessel designs against their intended routes, receiving terminals, and customer requirements to paying particular attention to propulsion, containment, and boil-off gas management. “Digital monitoring adds another layer of risk prevention, complementing crew expertise by helping identify potential issues before they develop into incidents,” notes Sun. “Systems on board cover real-time sloshing and hull-stress monitoring, collision avoidance, and engine-room monitoring and automation.” Celebration of Steel Cutting of LNG Carrier for SDME at Jiangnan Shipyard in February 2025, From left to right: Mao Zhenyu, Principal Surveyor, Jessia Li, Shanghai Station Manager, Kim, Tae Hyung, Principal Surveyor, Yuan Dan, Principal Surveyor/Project Manager for this one, Vincent Guenoden, Project Manager, Chen Keng, Area South Manager, Ren Xudong, Business Director This combination of technological and human-based risk prevention is underpinned by crew training and development at SDME. The ship management companies working with SDME conduct crew selection, training, simulator exercises, and pre-employment assessments. SDME has also established dedicated LNG training programmes and an LNG Vessel Intelligence and Innovation Laboratory with Shanghai Maritime University. “The essence of safety is getting every detail right. This is a common language throughout the LNG industry,” says Sun. Collaboration brings broad expertise into LNG projects This attention to detail also shapes SDME’s approach to new vessel technology. Its technical team becomes involved in newbuilding projects at an early stage, from developing specifications and reviewing key equipment selection to witnessing critical construction milestones. This enables technical decisions to be reviewed jointly with shipyards, class, and technology suppliers throughout the project. DNV plays a central technical role in this collaborative process, working with SDME on LNG carrier projects through plan approval and construction surveys, including oversight of containment and gas-handling systems and safety redundancy arrangements. DNV has also provided independent technical assessment and certification for technologies including dual-fuel engines, air lubrication, reliquefaction, and intelligent vessel systems, alongside regulatory support and regular technical exchanges. “This level of technical dialogue between owner, yard, technology suppliers, and class is particularly important when integrating multiple advanced systems into large LNG carrier designs, and we enjoyed a strong collaboration with SDME on this project,” says Xudong Ren, Business Director – Shipowner Development, Region Greater China, at DNV. Early technical dialogue supports QC-Max development SDME’s 271,000 cbm QC-Max newbuilds show why this early technical collaboration matters. “These exceptional vessel of this scale and five-tank configuration bring specific considerations for cargo containment, safety, and environmental performance,” notes Ren. During plan approval, SDME, the shipyard, supervision teams, and DNV held multiple rounds of technical discussions covering areas including the NO96 Super+ containment system, the shaft generator in power take-in (PTI) booster mode, reliquefaction system configuration, and the real-time sloshing monitoring system for the five-tank layout. “For a vessel of this scale, it is particularly important to resolve critical technical questions as early as possible,” Sun says. “Through discussions with DNV, the shipyard and the other parties involved, we were able to address key issues during the design and approval process rather than at a later, more costly stage of construction.” Independent third-party assessments support technology decisions Class-independent close collaboration has been applied to other technologies in the newbuilding programme. For the WinGD X-DF 2.2 dual-fuel engines selected for the 175,000 cbm LNG carriers, DNV provided an independent third-party evaluation of the technology. IMO Tier III NOx compliance in gas and diesel mode without exhaust after-treatment, and methane-slip reduction, were among the decision criteria. DNV has also evaluated the application of Silverstream air lubrication systems for several SDME projects. These assessments covered installation arrangements, operating boundary conditions, and compatibility with LNG cargo-handling systems, helping to ensure that efficiency improvements do not compromise vessel safety or cargo operations. Preparing LNG carriers for a tightening regulatory environment Alongside safety and efficiency, SDME is considering how today’s investment decisions will affect the fleet’s longer-term environmental performance. “We believe LNG has an important role to play as shipping moves towards lower and ultimately zero emissions,” says Sun. “One advantage is that the pathway does not necessarily end with fossil LNG. In the future, bio-LNG and synthetic e-LNG could provide further opportunities to reduce life-cycle emissions.” At the same time, SDME recognizes the commercial challenge created by evolving environmental requirements. Technologies for methane-slip reduction and energy-efficiency improvement can require further investment, while maintenance, fuel, and compliance costs also affect the business case. “This makes forward-looking fleet planning and continuous monitoring of environmental requirements increasingly important as we seek to combine regulatory compliance with competitive vessel performance and long-term asset value,” Sun points out. Collaboration supports the next generation of LNG shipping For SDME, developing its LNG carrier portfolio is about more than adding capacity. It is about building the technical and operational capabilities needed for increasingly advanced LNG shipping. As the company expands its presence in international LNG transportation, close collaboration with shipyards, technology suppliers, and class will remain important in bringing new technologies into operation safely and effectively. Equipment is installed, paperwork is filed, and the assumption takes hold that the safety obligation has been met. In the case of ATEX-certified cargo handling systems, that assumption is one of the more persistent, and consequential, misconceptions in maritime operations. ATEX (ATmosphères EXplosibles), derived from EU Directive 2014/34/EU, governs equipment used in potentially explosive environments: tankers, barges, bunkering units, and any vessel handling hydrocarbons or flammable cargoes. Its requirements extend across design, manufacture, and maintenance – covering the entire operational life of equipment installed in hazardous areas, not just the moment it leaves the yard. This distinction matters because compliance can be lost in service, often without any visible change in equipment performance. A non-genuine spare part, an uncertified technician, an undocumented repair – any of these can void ATEX certification while the system continues to operate normally. The obligation is not only to use certified equipment but to have it maintained by a certified service provider. Under the ADN inland waterway rules this is set out explicitly, and servicing by a company without ATEX certification can break compliance even where the work itself is sound, because the equipment can no longer be shown to meet the standard it was certified against. Bastiaan Idsinga, Manager Production and QHSE, MarFlex Operators frequently discover compliance failures not through routine oversight, but during port inspections, insurance claims, or following incidents. By that point, the consequences – detention, enforced retrofits, voided policies, and shifted liability – are already in motion. For UK-based operators, it is worth noting that following Brexit, equipment placed on the Great Britain market is now subject to the UKCA Ex conformity regime rather than ATEX directly. The underlying safety principles are identical, but the certification route differs. The operator’s responsibility remains the same: equipment must be installed, maintained, and documented in accordance with its certified design in order to remain compliant and insurable. The regulatory landscape is also shifting in ways that make proactive compliance planning increasingly important. Under the ADN 2023 Regulations, ATEX-certified deck equipment will be mandatory for all EU inland waterway vessels by the end of 2034, with retroactive application to existing tonnage. Many pre-2019 vessels lack the certified equipment or traceable documentation required to evidence compliance. As the deadline approaches, yard capacity and qualified service resource will come under pressure, making early action both operationally and commercially sensible. DNV’s Maritime Safety Trends 2014-2024 report recorded a 42% rise in fire and explosion incidents in the four years to 2024, part of a wider increase in casualties it attributes to an ageing fleet and machinery failure. That context helps explain why regulators and insurers are paying closer attention to hazardous-area compliance. The risk is not hypothetical, and it is not confined to UK or inland shipping. As charterer expectations around safety compliance tighten and port state control scrutiny increases globally, ATEX certification is increasingly relevant to commercial credibility as much as regulatory standing. Closing the compliance gap requires a structured approach to lifecycle management: certified service providers, genuine OEM parts, traceable documentation, and a forward-looking view of upgrade and recertification requirements. For fleet operators with older vessels, the 2034 deadline makes this especially pressing – yard availability and specialist resource will be constrained as the deadline approaches. MarFlex manufactures fully ATEX-certified electric-driven cargo, ballast, and pneumatic draining pumps for maritime, offshore, and industrial markets. With factory-level certification under Annex IV, Module D of Directive 2014/34/EU, every product is traceable from design through to post-sale service. Beyond equipment supply, MarFlex provides certified maintenance using genuine OEM parts, recertification for pre-2019 equipment, operator training, and structured pre-2034 compliance planning for fleet operators globally. The principle underpinning all of it is straightforward: compliance must be maintained and demonstrable at every point in a vessel’s life, not just at delivery. A certificate is where ATEX compliance begins. What happens next is an operational responsibility – and one that cannot be deferred indefinitely. articles.body: Battery Vessels Could Help Electrify Most of Global Shipping Emissions in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 24/11/2026 Battery-electric ships are economical only if the pack is cycled frequently, so they have been confined to short-sea, ferry and harbour vessels rather than the infrequently-berthing deep-sea fleet. Dedicated battery vessels (BVs) remove this limit by separating the battery from the host: coupling at or near a port and returning to port to recharge, they keep their packs cycling across many hosts. Using a gridded shipping- CO2 field and a geometric relay-corridor servability model, we map the global share BVs could serve. On a denominator of all shipping CO2(e), the battery-addressable share is about 62%, its servable corridors concentrated in European–Mediterranean and East and Southeast Asian waters. Because the coupling traffic hugs the coast, sea state is not the binding constraint. A screening cost model puts BV-delivered energy at breakeven with fuel oil near $173/tCO2e (well-to-wake basis) for a 20MW host and a future $100/kWh battery pack price, falling as host power rises. BVs thus reach the deep-sea fleet’s coastal legs that on-board batteries cannot. The maritime economy enters the latter part of 2026 after another period of disruption and adjustment. Trade continues to move through an increasingly complex global system, while maritime businesses face changing trade relationships and less predictable market conditions. Despite these pressures, the industry has continued to connect producers and consumers worldwide. It carries more than 80% of world trade by volume¹ and remains the most energy-efficient way to move goods over long distances. Its ability to adapt has again demonstrated the central role of maritime transport in the global economy. The changes extend well beyond shipping activity. Ports are responding to shifts in cargo flows and vessel deployment. Maritime service providers are helping businesses manage new commercial and regulatory demands. Technology companies and research institutions are supporting an industry undergoing both an energy and a digital transition. Recent trade figures illustrate this combination of resilience and uncertainty. Global goods trade reached approximately USD 13.7 trillion in the first half of 2026, an increase of 12.5% compared with the same period in 2025. Services trade grew by 10.5%². Part of this increase reflected higher prices, however, and performance varied considerably between regions and sectors. Global trade therefore remains active, but its growth is increasingly uneven and exposed to geopolitical and economic pressures. For the maritime sector, the direction and composition of trade now matter as much as its overall value. Geopolitical uncertainty and disruption at maritime chokepoints are influencing trade relationships, voyage patterns and the configuration of supply chains. Regional decarbonisation requirements are shaping operational and investment decisions, while future global regulatory pathways remain uncertain. Digitalisation is creating opportunities to improve efficiency and decision-making, but also introduces new requirements for data, systems and cybersecurity. These developments are also changing the capabilities required across the maritime sector. Businesses increasingly need professionals who can combine maritime knowledge with expertise in technology, new fuels, regulation, finance and risk management. The ability to attract international expertise, develop local capabilities and support movement between maritime roles is therefore becoming more relevant to the competitiveness of maritime cities. Together, these shifts are broadening the basis of maritime competitiveness. Strategic location, port capacity and shipping activity remain essential, but they are not sufficient on their own. Maritime businesses also need access to capital, specialised services, technology networks and skilled people. They benefit most from clusters in which these capabilities reinforce one another. The maritime landscape in 2026 and beyond is therefore defined by continued activity alongside significant transition. Global trade remains resilient, but the environment supporting it is becoming more demanding and unpredictable. The strongest maritime cities will be those that can support current maritime activity while preparing their ecosystem for longer-term changes in trade, regulation, technology and workforce needs. articles.title: IMO faces tough compromise on shipping emissions rules amid US opposition
articles.summary: The International Maritime Organization faces another difficult round of negotiations over the Net-Zero Framework from late November, with countries seeking a compromise on the contentious carbon pricing mechanism that could determine the pace of shipping’s transition to low-carbon fuels. articles.body: IMO faces tough compromise on shipping emissions rules amid US opposition in International Shipping News 24/11/2026 The International Maritime Organization faces another difficult round of negotiations over the Net-Zero Framework from late November, with countries seeking a compromise on the contentious carbon pricing mechanism that could determine the pace of shipping’s transition to low-carbon fuels. While industry participants see growing agreement on the framework’s technical requirements for marine energy’s greenhouse gas emissions intensity, deep divisions remain over how ships should comply with the GHG standards, whether mandatory payments should be imposed for non-compliance, and how any revenues should be distributed. The UN agency’s member states will meet Nov. 23-27 for technical negotiations, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session on Nov. 30-Dec. 3. An extraordinary session could resume Dec. 4 to consider adopting the framework. The meetings follow a decision in October 2025 to postpone adoption for a year amid fierce US opposition to what Washington describes as a global carbon tax. “I think it’s very hard to predict [the outcome],” Lloyd’s Register CEO Nick Brown told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. “Most of the concern is around the commercial instrument, because we don’t really have any experience of a global carbon tax that is applied across all countries, and how it is collected, and then what happens to the money.” He suggested that governments could initially introduce technical requirements while gradually implementing financial measures. “Maybe the economic measures could be introduced or phased in or ramped up over time,” Brown said. Countries seek compromise The framework approved in April 2025 combines progressively tightening GHG intensity thresholds from 2028 with financial penalties for ships failing to meet the requirements. Under the original proposal, companies could comply by using lower-emission fuels, acquiring surplus units from other ships or purchasing remedial units, with payments directed into an IMO-managed fund. The US has opposed mandatory payments, arguing that they would increase shipping costs and consumer inflation. US Federal Maritime Commission Chairman Laura DiBella told Platts Nov. 11 that she expected countries to move toward consensus, although final rules might not be codified until 2027. “I don’t think anything will be codified this year — maybe 2027 it will be codified. But I think we’ll come to some sort of consensus,” DiBella said. Several countries have proposed alternative compliance arrangements. China has suggested using multipliers to encourage uptake of zero or near-zero emission fuels, while Norway has proposed similar initiatives. In separate proposals, Japan, Djibouti, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Somalia and Yemen have suggested ships could meet obligations through investments in maritime decarbonization projects rather than mandatory penalties. Most EU and Pacific Island states continue to support the existing framework, although divisions have emerged within Europe. Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Malta have called for pragmatic, cost-effective global measures, while Union of Greek Shipowners President Melina Travlos accused the EU of taking an uncompromising position that risked another negotiating deadlock. “The EU’s uncompromising position is steering the IMO process to a new dead end,” Travlos said in a Nov. 16 statement, questioning whether Brussels is more interested in preserving revenues generated from its Emissions Trading System for shipping and FuelEU maritime rather than pursuing a global framework. The European Commission did not respond to emails seeking comment. Compliance dilemma Edmund Hughes, the International Bunker Industry Association’s representative to the IMO, said the central challenge was establishing a workable compliance mechanism for ships unable to obtain alternative fuels or sufficient surplus units. “You can’t leave that void. It’s a void at the moment, and that’s where the impasse is … in the negotiation,” Hughes told Platts. “If you have a technical standard, you have to find a way to comply with it.” Hughes said negotiators were attempting to balance environmental ambitions, commercial realities and political demands while preserving a framework acceptable to enough member states. A coalition of nine shipping associations, including BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping, IBIA and INTERTANKO, has urged governments to agree on enforceable global regulations that provide investment certainty and flexible compliance options. The groups warned that fragmented regional rules could impose overlapping obligations and additional costs on shipping companies. Separately, a group of shipowners, maritime associations and flag registries has called for an alternative global emissions framework that takes into account the availability and affordability of cleaner fuels, technological readiness and potential impacts on international trade. The statement, circulated to media by Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry, was accompanied by a list of supporters that the ministry said represented approximately 55% of the international merchant fleet. The ministry stressed that the statement was industry-led and did not represent Saudi Arabia’s official position. Environmental organizations, however, have cautioned against diluting the framework. “The biggest danger at MEPC 85 is no longer delay, but a rushed deal designed to get Trump and his allies to the table,” said Alex Springer, deputy director of shipping at Transport & Environment. Springer warned that concessions favoring fossil LNG and crop-based biofuels could prolong shipping’s dependence on fossil fuels. Clean Shipping Coalition President Lucas Leppert urged countries to adopt the framework before year-end, arguing that further delays would undermine climate action. Fuel demand implications Whether and how IMO member states design the framework’s financial elements could affect the uptake of sustainable fuels, which remain more expensive than conventional, oil-based fuels due to limited availability. October’s average delivered bunker costs in Singapore were $22.78/gigajoule for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil, compared with $27/GJ for B24 biofuel blends, $28.48/GJ for LNG and $48.47/GJ for 100% sustainable methanol, according to the Platts global bunker cost calculator. “No shipping company is going to carry on buying more expensive fuel while their competitors are not,” Hughes said. “You need some way of closing that price gap.” S&P Global Energy’s October 2026 Global Alternative Bunker Fuels Long-Term Outlook forecasts conventional fuel oil and gasoil’s share of bunker energy demand declining from 85% in 2030 to 26% by 2060, with shipping companies shifting to alternative fuels. “The market is likely to follow the most cost-effective pathway, resulting in a bias towards LNG-fuelled ships,” according to the outlook. “If conditions are right, parts of this fleet could migrate to ammonia fuel later in the forecast.” Source: Platts 2026-11-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Fuel Switch Snapshot: Rotterdam’s B100 loses its discount to VLSFO in International Shipping News 24/11/2026 B100 and liquefied biomethane (LBM) have both lost ground to conventional fuels for intra-EU voyages from Rotterdam over the past week. Lower FuelEU pooling values have added to rises in both fuels’ prices. OceanScore’s FuelEU pooling index has fallen by €4.40/mtCO2e ($5/mtCO2e) to €78.75/mtCO2e ($87/mtCO2e) over the past week. This has cut the potential pooling value of B100’s compliance surplus by $16/mt in Rotterdam, adding to the fuel’s $68/mt rise. Rotterdam’s B100 has flipped from an $86/mt discount to VLSFO to a $34/mt premium over it, and from a $23/mt discount to B30-VLSFO to a $128/mt premium over the blend. Its discount to B30-LSMGO has narrowed by $129/mt to $273/mt over the past week. B100’s discount to LSMGO has narrowed by $189/mt to $301/mt, partly driven by a $121/mt slump in Rotterdam’s LSMGO price. LBM remains the priciest fuel option for intra-EU voyages from Rotterdam for vessels with either engine type. It has gained $69-76/mt depending on engine type over the past week, with a $16-19/mt decline in the potential pooling value of LBM’s compliance surplus adding to the rise. LBM’s premiums over VLSFO have widened by $122-128/mt to $594-700/mt depending on engine type over the past week. Its premiums over LSMGO have widened by $190-197/mt to $259-365/mt. Liquid fuels Rotterdam’s HSFO, VLSFO and LSMGO prices have fallen by $34-121/mt over the past week, with LSMGO down the most. B30-VLSFO has dropped by $84/mt and B30-LSMGO has fallen by a smaller $61/mt. Prompt availability of conventional fuels has been tight in ARA ports, with lead times of 5-7 days recommended for good coverage from suppliers, a trader said. Dutch ZRE A tickets have fallen by €30/mtCO2e ($34/mtCO2e) to €170/mtCO2e ($187/mtCO2e) over the past week. In Singapore, HSFO, VLSFO and LSMGO prices have fallen by $32-95/mt, with LSMGO down the most. B100 has fallen by $59/mt. Bunker fuel availability has remained tight in Singapore, with terminal loading schedules and barge capacity heavily booked for most suppliers throughout November. Some suppliers have already made bookings for dates in December, a source said. Liquid gases Rotterdam’s LBM prices have outpaced LNG, with the latter up $42-48/mt depending on engine type in the past week. For vessels with Otto medium speed (Otto MS) engines, LBM’s premium over LNG has widened by $28/mt to $79/mt. For vessels with diesel slow speed (diesel SS) engines, it has widened by $28/mt to $75/mt. Singapore’s LNG prices have fallen by $56-59/mt depending on engine type. LNG premiums over VLSFO in the port have narrowed by $24-27/mt to $341-391/mt. On the other hand, Singapore LNG premiums over LSMGO have widened by $36-39/mt to $127-177/mt. Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news 2026-11-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Lufthansa Cargo has signed an agreement to acquire Fiege Air Cargo Logistics (FACL), bringing cargo handling operations at its Frankfurt hub under direct management. The agreement was signed on 20 November 2026 with Fiege Logistik Stiftung & Co. KG, the current owner of FACL. The proposed acquisition remains subject to antitrust and regulatory approvals. Once completed, Lufthansa Cargo will take responsibility for cargo handling at the Lufthansa Cargo Center in Frankfurt. The move is part of the airline’s wider strategy to improve operational efficiency and strengthen its position in the global air freight market. Fiege to remain a strategic partner Although Lufthansa Cargo plans to take over FACL, its long-standing partnership with Fiege will continue. Under the new arrangement, Fiege will focus on recruiting, training and providing specialised personnel for cargo handling operations. The two companies have worked together since 2020, when Lufthansa Cargo transferred part of its physical cargo handling activities in Frankfurt to FACL. “We offer our customers high-quality and reliable solutions. Frankfurt is the most important hub in our network,” said Frank Bauer, Chief Operations Officer, Lufthansa Cargo. “Taking full responsibility for handling operations is a logical step in this regard,” Bauer added. According to Lufthansa Cargo, bringing operations under its own management will make it easier to introduce new technologies and accelerate warehouse automation. The transition will take place gradually following regulatory approval. Employment conditions for existing staff will remain unchanged during the process. Acquisition supports wider growth strategy The planned transaction follows Lufthansa Cargo’s recent acquisition of LUG aircargo handling, which expanded its ground handling capacity in Germany. The airline is also investing €600 million in modernising the Lufthansa Cargo Center in Frankfurt. These developments form part of its ambition to return to the world’s three largest air cargo providers by 2030. Lufthansa Cargo aims to strengthen its handling infrastructure, improve operational flexibility and expand automation across its facilities. The financial terms of the proposed FACL acquisition have not been disclosed.

Join the leading maritime news network ImagineStock / Shutterstock Spain will ban wastewater discharges from ship exhaust gas cleaning systems, commonly known as scrubbers, in its ports and internal waters beginning July 1, 2027, imposing restrictions that go beyond existing regional environmental requirements. The measure, established under Royal Decree 1006/2026 and published November 20, applies to all civilian vessels regardless of flag. It covers discharges from open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid scrubber systems in Spanish internal waters, port areas and designated anchorages. Scrubbers allow ships to meet International Maritime Organization (IMO) sulfur emissions limits while continuing to burn higher-sulfur fuel oil. However, the systems can generate wastewater containing heavy metals, hydrocarbons and other pollutants. The new rules implement a 2025 decision by the OSPAR Commission, which oversees marine environmental protection in the Northeast Atlantic. That agreement requires participating countries to prohibit open-loop scrubber discharges in ports and internal waters by July 2027, with restrictions extending to all scrubber operating modes by July 2029. Spain has chosen to accelerate the broader prohibition by two years and extend it nationwide, including to Mediterranean ports outside the OSPAR region. The ban does not prohibit scrubber use or apply across all Spanish territorial waters. Instead, vessels must stop discharging wastewater before entering restricted areas, either switching to compliant low-sulfur fuel or retaining wastewater onboard where technically possible. Spain already restricts scrubber discharges at several major ports, including Algeciras, Barcelona, Cartagena and Valencia. The decree establishes a common national standard. Spanish shipowners’ association ANAVE has criticized the accelerated timetable and broader geographic scope, calling for greater alignment with IMO guidelines. In its statement, ANAVE questioned whether Spain had adequately justified the additional restrictions through environmental risk assessments. It also raised concerns about the availability of port reception facilities for wastewater from closed-loop systems. The association noted that shipowners have invested heavily in scrubber technology under existing international regulations and warned against measures that undermine regulatory certainty. The decree also introduces reporting and inspection requirements. Scrubber-equipped ships must notify Spanish authorities of their systems at least 24 hours before arrival, or upon departure from the previous port for shorter voyages. Authorities may inspect fuel-changeover records and scrubber operating logs. Spain’s move reflects growing pressure to restrict scrubber wastewater discharges even as the technology remains an accepted method of meeting IMO air pollution standards. U.S. Central Command/Handout via REUTERS The U.S. Treasury Department on Monday announced new sanctions targeting financial networks supporting Iran’s oil exports and tanker operations, including companies accused of facilitating payments for the National Iranian Tanker Company (NITC) and shipping arrangements linked to the Iranian military. The latest action , announced under Operation Economic Outcast, targets 22 entities and eight individuals involved in moving billions of dollars through Iran’s international financial networks. Unlike previous sanctions rounds focused on tankers and shipping companies, the latest measures target the financial infrastructure that allows Iran to collect oil revenues and pay for maritime services despite U.S. restrictions. Among those designated is Dubai-based OGA Global General Trading LLC, which Treasury said facilitated millions of dollars in payments for NITC, Iran’s state-owned tanker operator. Treasury also identified a tanker chartering arrangement involving the SERENE I (IMO 9197832). According to the department, Dubai-based H N B Trading Co LLC facilitated payment for the vessel’s charter involving Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company, an Iranian military-linked entity, and sanctioned shipping company Dragon Road Ltd. Other targets include Dubai-based Gespl International General Trading LLC, accused of facilitating oil and petrochemical sales for the National Iranian Oil Company, and Integral Petro Energy Trading LLC, which allegedly facilitated millions of dollars in liquefied petroleum gas sales involving Kharg Petrochemical Company. The sanctions also target the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, which Treasury described as a central mechanism for connecting Iranian exporters earning foreign currency with importers seeking funds for overseas purchases. The institution reportedly supports tens of billions of dollars in annual trade, including transactions using Chinese yuan and Russian rubles. The action comes just days after Treasury claimed that no Iranian oil had been loaded onto vessels since Operation Economic Outcast began on August 24 and that no Iranian oil remained afloat outside the U.S. military blockade. Under U.S. sanctions rules, assets belonging to designated entities within U.S. jurisdiction are blocked, while foreign financial institutions may face additional sanctions exposure for facilitating certain transactions involving those entities. articles.body: Maersk will reduce its Peak Season Surcharge (PSS) for dry container shipments from the Indian Subcontinent to the US and Canadian East and Gulf coasts. The revised charges will apply from 24 November 2026 to non-SPOT bookings. For shipments from Nhava Sheva, Mundra, Pipavav, Hazira, Nepal and Bhutan to covered ports other than Houston, the surcharge will be US$2,650 for a 20-foot dry container and US$2,950 for 40-foot dry, 40-foot high-cube and 45-foot high-cube equipment. Cargo originating in South and East India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and the Maldives will face a surcharge of US$3,100 per container to covered destinations other than Houston. Maersk will apply a separate US$4,800 surcharge to shipments from India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Nepal and Bhutan bound for Houston. articles.body: Oil Prices Fall As Middle East Flows Increase Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 23, 2026 © Adobe Stock/le Oil prices fell on Monday as a rise in supplies from the Middle East and the restart of a Libyan oil pipeline offset unease about persistent shipping and refinery attacks in the region. Brent crude futures fell $2.02, or 2.18%, to $90.55 a barrel by 1436 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures were down $1.59, or 1.91%, at $81.82 a barrel. Earlier in the session, both contracts fell by more than 3%, with Brent hitting its lowest level in two weeks at $89.48 a barrel while WTI fell to its lowest since August 27 at $80.55. Libya's Sharara oil pipeline has reopened and crude is beginning to flow into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya, the chairman of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Monday. Meanwhile, JPMorgan expects oil futures to fall to the high $70s in the first half of 2027 due to an estimated supply surplus, with higher Middle East production outside Iran next year along with more supply from the Americas led by the US. Bank of America said geopolitics would remain the key driver of oil prices, with relatively low global inventories leaving much of the world vulnerable to supply disruptions. "It is partly the growing signs of a glut, but with each passing day it seems less likely that Trump will attack again," said IG chief market analyst Chris Beauchamp. On Sunday, however, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement said it attacked a Saudi Arabian oil refinery, while the UK Maritime Trade Operations reported multiple attacks on shipping in the Gulf and near the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend. Bahrain said an Iranian attack hit a civilian industrial facility on Saturday, while Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had launched a missile-and-drone assault on US military positions in the kingdom, home to the US Navy's 5th Fleet. "It would be irresponsible to conclude that oil will now be supplied uninterruptedly and in vast volumes. Iranian attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz are taking their toll," said PVM analyst Tamas Varga. In Turkey, talks on Sunday at the global climate conference COP31 collapsed for the first time since 2009 after nations could not agree on a deal on including a statement on the phase-out of fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing countries have said fossil fuels will play a role in the economy for the foreseeable future and they lobbied to keep any mention of fossil fuels out of the text, observers at the conference said. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group is made up of OPEC and other oil producers such as Russia. (Reuters)

articles.title: Russia to Spend $576m on Kaliningrad Supply Ferries
articles.summary: Russia will spend 47 billion roubles ($576 million) to build two giant rail ferries to ensure uninterrupted supplies to its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad amid rising tensions in the region, Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said on Monday.Kaliningrad…
articles.body: Russia to Spend $576m on Kaliningrad Supply Ferries Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 23, 2026 © andriano_cz - stock.adobe.com Russia will spend 47 billion roubles ($576 million) to build two giant rail ferries to ensure uninterrupted supplies to its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad amid rising tensions in the region, Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said on Monday. Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave located between EU and NATO members Poland and Lithuania, has become increasingly reliant on the sea route since 2022, after Lithuania banned transit of many goods, including construction materials, through its territory in compliance with the EU sanctions against Russia. "Kaliningrad region has a special geography, and due to the unlawful actions of certain countries, disruptions to logistics chains and attempts at a transport blockade are complicating the operations of enterprises located there," Mishustin said. The two ferries are expected to go into operation in 2030 and operate between the port of Ust-Luga in Russia's Leningrad region and Baltiysk in Kaliningrad. Most of the money will come from Russia's rainy-day fund, Mishustin said. The announcement comes after Sparta II, a Russian cargo ship with links to the military that transported cargo to Kaliningrad, was hit by drones and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, in what Finland's military said was likely an attack by Ukraine, highlighting growing security risks in the region. Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said on November 21 that a drone alert went off in a district bordering Lithuania after an appearance of a "suspicious object." In a document sent to NATO in September, Russia warned NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad. Maritime shipping now accounts for over half of supplies to Kaliningrad, compared with just 8% in 2021, before the war in Ukraine started. About 30 ships, including four rail ferries, now transport goods between the exclave and Russian ports on the Baltic Sea. ($1 = 81.5841 roubles) (Reuters)

articles.title: Arc to Supply Power Management, Electrical Systems for USV Defiant
articles.summary: Arc, a marine technology company, announced it has been selected to provide the power management and electrical systems for USX-1 Defiant, the unmanned surface vessel developed under the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency's (DARPA) No Manning Required Ship (NOMARS) program.
articles.body: Arc to Supply Power Management, Electrical Systems for USV Defiant Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 23, 2026 The NOMARS program’s demonstration vessel, USX-1 Defiant, completed construction in February 2025. Source: DARPA | Colie Wertz Arc, a marine technology company, announced it has been selected to provide the power management and electrical systems for USX-1 Defiant , the unmanned surface vessel developed under the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency's (DARPA) No Manning Required Ship (NOMARS) program. Under the funded agreement, Arc Boats will integrate the vessel's high-voltage power management hardware and software, bringing the company's commercial electrification expertise into an autonomous maritime program. Defiant is a technology demonstrator designed to prove that a ship can operate reliably without a crew. The vessel has no berthing, galley, or life-support systems on board, allowing it to remain at sea, fully unmanned, for up to 90 days. Arc Boats is developing and integrating the vessel's electrical backbone—a fault-tolerant, self-healing DC-power system that autonomously monitors diagnostic information and can resolve without human intervention. Arc Boats’ architecture also enables remote startup of high-voltage systems, a process that once required a technician. For a vessel operating unmanned for months at sea, autonomy is the difference between a mission that succeeds and one that ends early. Arc Boats’ experience translates directly to the reliability and redundancy demands of unmanned maritime platforms. As part of the agreement, the company will advise DARPA throughout system integration, helping shape an electrical architecture designed to support future defense applications. The defense sector is increasingly investing in crewless maritime platforms across a range of programs. These programs share a common need for more capable powertrains—ones that deliver extended range, greater reliability, and software-defined control. Moving from mechanical to electrical architectures like the ones developed by Arc Boats delivers those improved capabilities. As adoption of unmanned platforms accelerates, dependable power infrastructure won't just support long-duration, crewless missions, it will determine whether the mission is possible at all. Arc Boats’ work on Defiant marks another step in bringing its advanced integrated power systems into critical defense applications.

articles.title: Iranian Floating Crude Storage Drops to Under 4 Million Barrels
articles.summary: Iran’s floating crude storage in Asia is nearly gone. Windward put Iranian crude stored on tankers off Malaysia at about 70 million barrels in January, and at most about 3.8 million barrels remain. The tankers that delivered that crude are sitting empty off Sri Lanka.
articles.body: Iranian Floating Crude Storage Drops to Under 4 Million Barrels Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 23, 2026 Iranian floating storage at the Singapore/Malaysia EOPL anchorage, January to November 20, 2026. Source: Windward Iran’s floating crude storage in Asia is nearly gone. Windward put Iranian crude stored on tankers off Malaysia at about 70 million barrels in January, and at most about 3.8 million barrels remain. The tankers that delivered that crude are sitting empty off Sri Lanka. As the stock in Asia runs out, a larger Iranian attempt to move crude past the U.S. blockade becomes more likely. Iran’s crude buffer in Asia sits on tankers at Malaysia’s Eastern Outer Port Limits (EOPL) anchorage. After Windward's January prediction, it was about 30 million barrels in late March. On 12 July, Windward tracked nine sanctioned Iranian tankers at EOPL with AIS off, holding about 14.6 million barrels. As of November 20, only two Iran-linked VLCCs at the anchorage were last reported laden: M.T HEDY (IMO 9212888) on June 19 and FIONA II (IMO 9262766) on September 11. Together they hold at most about 3.8 million barrels. The tankers that carried that crude have not gone back to Iran for more. On August 30, Windward flagged 21 Iran-flagged ships drifting off Sri Lanka, 20 of them empty crude tankers. Nearly three months later they are still there. On November 20, 20 sanctioned tankers, 18 of them VLCCs, were at ballast draught off Sri Lanka, which indicates they are empty. Sentinel-2 satellite imagery from the same day shows a tanker at 19 of their 20 AIS positions. That is about 38 million barrels of empty capacity waiting for the U.S. blockade to open. The pressure on Iran to move crude is building. The first attempt to cross the blockade line will likely come from tankers that are already loaded and close. Four laden crude tankers carrying an estimated 4.9 million barrels are between the Strait of Hormuz and the line, within about a day’s sailing of it. As the stock in Asia runs out, a larger crude push becomes more likely. Sanctioned VLCCs at the EOPL anchorage on satellite imagery. Only M.T HEDY and FIONA II last reported laden. (TSGI) have announced that both companies are now 100% employee owned through an Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP), marking a milestone for the two naval architecture and marine engineering firms. For Gregory W. Beers, P.E., and Cory C. Wood, who founded BHGI in 1995 and later established TSGI in 2010, the transition represents the continuation of a vision that began more than three decades ago. Through planning, the development of strong management teams and a continued investment in their employees, they have positioned both firms to become multigenerational leaders in the naval architecture and marine engineering industry. The transition to employee ownership is a step in securing that future, ensuring that the companies they founded continue to grow and succeed for generations to come. While ownership has changed, both firms will continue operating much as they have for years. Gregory and Cory will remain at the forefront of both companies, providing leadership and direction alongside their established management teams. Clients can continue to expect the same level of service and technical expertise from the employees they've come to know and trust over the years. With the ESOP now in place, Gregory will serve as Chairman and President, Cory as Vice Chairman, and Joshua as Vice President of both BHGI and TSGI. The engineering teams will continue under the direction of Daniel at BHGI and Harrison at TSGI, both as Engineering Managers. BHGI's History BHGI traces its origins back to 1993, when Gregory and Cory, along with Andy Tyska of Bristol Marine and another fellow student at the University of Michigan Naval Architecture and Marine Engineering Department, set out to design a passenger vessel while still in school. Their first design, the STAR OF SAUGATUCK Il, marked an early milestone for the firm and is still operating on the Kalamazoo River in Southwest Michigan. Building on that early initiative, the group formally incorporated BHGI in 1995, and the firm has continued to grow in Bristol, Rhode Island, ever since. TSGI's History In 2010, Gregory and Cory formed The Shearer Group, Inc. (TSGI), a sister company to BHGI located in Houston, Texas. The company was established when Gregory and Cory purchased the assets of Shearer & Assoc., Inc. from Edward L. Shearer, P.E., its founder and president. The three had heard of one another through industry connections and eventually met at a SNAME convention. That encounter led to further discussions, and ultimately the formation of TSGI. The "Shearer" name has long been associated with the inland marine industry, reflecting both Ed's contributions to naval architecture and his family's multigenerational barge line. When TSGI was established, it brought together Ed's years of experience at Shearer & Associates, Inc. and the naval architecture and marine engineering expertise Gregory and Cory had developed at BHGI. Ed remains involved as a Principal Naval Architect. Today, TSGI provides marine engineering services to clients in the inland and offshore marine industries. The firm offers many of the same services as BHGl, along with additional services suited to its Houston location, including marine surveying and OSHA-compliant maritime gear certification support.

REUTERS/Alessandro Bianchi Francesco Schettino, the former captain of the Costa Concordia cruise ship that capsized off Italy in 2012, killing 32 people, has been released from prison after more than nine years behind bars. Schettino, 66, left Rome’s Rebibbia prison Friday evening after a supervisory court approved his request to serve the remainder of his sentence under the supervision of social services, according to Italian news agency ANSA. The decision follows a review of his conduct and participation in rehabilitation programs during his imprisonment. Schettino was sentenced to 16 years and one month for his role in the January 13, 2012, disaster, when the Costa Concordia struck rocks near the Italian island of Giglio during an unauthorized close-to-shore maneuver. The collision opened a massive gash in the vessel’s hull, causing flooding and a loss of power. The ship eventually capsized near the island, triggering a chaotic nighttime evacuation of more than 4,200 passengers and crew. Schettino became the focus of international outrage after leaving the vessel before the evacuation was complete. Investigators also identified delays in ordering passengers to abandon ship. He was convicted of multiple manslaughter, causing a shipwreck and abandoning ship. Italy’s highest court upheld his prison sentence in May 2017 , prompting his immediate imprisonment. Under the newly approved arrangement, Schettino will live in southern Italy’s Campania region, where he is expected to work eight hours a day in an administrative position with a private employer. He must also perform weekly volunteer work and comply with restrictions on his movements, including remaining at home overnight. According to ANSA, good-conduct credits have also advanced his projected sentence completion date to July 2030, approximately two years earlier than previously expected. The Costa Concordia disaster remains one of the deadliest cruise ship accidents in modern history. The wreck was righted in 2013 and refloated in 2014 before being towed to Genoa for dismantling, ending one of the most complex salvage operations ever undertaken. Schettino’s release comes less than two months before the 15th anniversary of the disaster. Finnish Border Guard/Handout via REUTERS The Russian cargo ship Sparta II , severely damaged in a suspected Ukrainian drone attack in the Gulf of Finland, has been towed out of Finnish waters following a multinational firefighting operation, Finnish President Alexander Stubb confirmed. The departure came despite a temporary sanctions-related restriction imposed by Finnish authorities after determining that the vessel belonged to a company subject to European Union sanctions. “The Russian vessel, Sparta II, has now left Finnish territorial waters. In its current state it posed a serious danger in the Gulf of Finland,” Stubb said in a statement Sunday. “Unfortunately, the consequences of Russia’s war of aggression are also visible in our region,” he added, thanking Finnish authorities for their handling of the incident. The Russian-flagged cargo ship was struck by drones Saturday while sailing through international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, en route from St. Petersburg to Kaliningrad. The attack sparked a fire aboard the 121-meter vessel, which subsequently lost maneuverability and drifted into Finnish territorial waters near Loviisa. All 16 crew members were evacuated onto another Russian vessel. One reportedly suffered minor injuries. Finnish defense officials have assessed that Ukraine was likely responsible for the attack, although Kyiv has not publicly claimed responsibility. In a statement Monday , Finland’s National Enforcement Authority confirmed that it had investigated the vessel’s connections to sanctioned entities after the ship entered Finnish waters. The agency determined that Sparta II belonged to a company on the EU sanctions list and imposed a temporary enforcement measure at 8 p.m. Saturday. The measure prohibited the vessel’s release but specifically allowed exceptions when necessary for maritime rescue operations, safety or the reduction of environmental risks. The vessel is operated by Oboronlogistika, a Russian shipping company linked to the country’s Ministry of Defense and involved in transporting military cargo. Ultimately, Finnish authorities allowed the damaged ship to be towed away, citing the risks associated with keeping the vessel in Finnish waters. The rescue operation involved vessels from Finland, Estonia and Russia working together to control the fire and prevent an environmental disaster. According to the Finnish Border Guard , the Russian rescue vessel Murman began towing Sparta II on Sunday, assisted by the Finnish patrol vessel Uisko , the Estonian Navy’s Kindral Kurvits and rescue tugs operated by Alfons Håkans. By Sunday afternoon, thermal imaging showed that some containers aboard the ship remained hot, although flames were no longer visible externally. The vessel was listing slightly but remained stable enough to be towed. Finnish authorities reported no detected leakage of fuel or hazardous substances. The ship subsequently departed Finnish territorial waters and the country’s maritime rescue responsibility area, ending Finland’s direct involvement in the operation. The incident has highlighted growing concerns over the spillover of the Russia-Ukraine war into the Baltic Sea, where attacks against Russian military and logistics assets have increasingly occurred near NATO territory. The Kremlin on Monday accused Ukraine of engaging in what it described as terrorist activity in the Baltic Sea and urged countries in the region to discourage further attacks. articles.title: FedEx-led consortium completes acquisition of InPost
articles.summary: A consortium comprising Advent International, FedEx, A&R Investments and PPF Group has completed its acquisition of European parcel delivery company InPost. The transaction, announced on 20 November 2026, brings InPost under private ownership. The company has also been delisted from Euronext Amsterdam. Under the new...
articles.body: A consortium comprising Advent International, FedEx, A&R Investments and PPF Group has completed its acquisition of European parcel delivery company InPost. The transaction, announced on 20 November 2026, brings InPost under private ownership. The company has also been delisted from Euronext Amsterdam. Under the new ownership structure, Advent International and FedEx each hold 37% of the consortium. A&R Investments owns 16%, while PPF Group holds the remaining 10%. InPost will continue operating independently under its existing brand. Its headquarters will remain in Poland, with founder Rafał Brzoska staying on as CEO alongside the current management team. FedEx and InPost target European delivery growth The acquisition brings together FedEx’s global logistics network and InPost’s extensive European parcel delivery infrastructure. InPost operates more than 100,000 out-of-home delivery locations, including over 70,000 automated parcel lockers and close to 30,000 pick-up and drop-off points. The consortium plans to accelerate investment in this network, with further expansion targeted across the United Kingdom, Italy, France, Spain, Portugal and the Benelux region. The investment will also support improvements to InPost’s digital services and customer experience. Meanwhile, FedEx and InPost are exploring opportunities to connect their services more closely. The companies have already entered into separate commercial agreements that allow selected recipients to use InPost’s last-mile delivery services and out-of-home infrastructure in Europe. These arrangements could eventually provide FedEx customers with additional delivery options through InPost’s European network. “Connecting our global network of 3 million businesses and 225 million recipients with InPost’s last-mile capabilities gives both businesses a potential springboard for profitable growth,” said Raj Subramaniam, President and CEO of FedEx. “We see significant opportunity to expand our commercial arrangements across Europe and look forward to building on it as members of the Consortium,” Subramaniam added. Brzoska said the new ownership structure would provide the capital and expertise needed to support InPost’s continued expansion. The acquisition follows the consortium’s initial agreement, announced in February 2026, to acquire InPost through an all-cash offer of €15.60 per share. With the transaction now completed, InPost will focus on expanding its European delivery network while maintaining its independent operations.
